public.prompt: A line graph plots the measured points and then draws a line connecting them. What does the connecting line make easier to see?

options.text: How the values rose, fell, or stayed the same over time
The total sum of all the measured values
Which individual point is the highest outlier
How many distinct categories the data contains

opt_trend.message: Correct. The connecting line makes it easier to see how values rose, fell, or stayed the same over time — the slope between adjacent points shows the direction of change at a glance.

opt_total.message: Not quite. The line connects measured points in order; it does not accumulate or sum them. A bar chart or a running total would show sums.

opt_outlier.message: Not quite. The connecting line reveals the trend across all points, not just the highest one. Outliers are visible as individual points regardless of whether a line is drawn.

opt_category.message: Not quite. A line graph is for ordered numeric data over time, not for counting categories. A bar chart is the right tool for comparing discrete categories.

correct.message: Right. The line between adjacent points makes rises and falls immediately readable — that is the whole point of connecting them.

incorrect.message: A line graph plots measured points and draws a line connecting them in order. That line makes it easier to see how values rose, fell, or stayed the same over time.

hints: Think about what you can read from the slope of the line between two adjacent points.
The fact says the line makes it easier to see something 'over time' — what changes over time?

public.prompt: A box plot of Lagos delivery times has Q1 = 20 minutes and Q3 = 30 minutes. The IQR is 10 minutes. A delivery of 50 minutes is recorded. How will matplotlib draw that 50-minute delivery?

options.text: As a flier point (outlier) beyond the upper whisker
At the tip of the upper whisker
Inside the box, between Q1 and Q3
It is ignored and not drawn

opt_flier.message: Correct. The upper whisker can reach at most Q3 + 1.5 × IQR = 30 + 15 = 45 minutes. A 50-minute delivery is beyond that limit, so it is drawn as a separate flier point.

opt_whisker.message: Not quite. The whisker tip is the farthest data point that still falls within 1.5 × IQR of the box (at most 45 minutes here). A 50-minute delivery exceeds that limit and is drawn as a flier point.

opt_box.message: Not quite. The box spans Q1 to Q3 (20 to 30 minutes). A 50-minute delivery is far above Q3 and would be drawn as a flier point beyond the upper whisker.

opt_ignored.message: Not quite. Matplotlib draws all data points. Values beyond 1.5 × IQR from the box are shown as individual flier points — they are not ignored.

correct.message: Right. The upper whisker reaches at most Q3 + 1.5 × IQR = 45 minutes. The 50-minute delivery exceeds that, so it appears as a flier point.

incorrect.message: The whiskers extend to the farthest point within 1.5 × IQR of the box. Here that is Q3 + 1.5 × 10 = 45 minutes. A 50-minute delivery is beyond that limit and is drawn as a separate flier point.

hints: Calculate the upper whisker limit: Q3 + 1.5 × IQR = 30 + 1.5 × 10 = ?

opt_box.message: Correct. Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing the distributions of multiple datasets side by side — showing the median, spread, and outliers for each city in a single figure.

opt_bar.message: Not quite. A bar chart shows one value per category (such as the mean). It does not show the spread, quartiles, or outliers of each city's distribution — a box plot does.

opt_line.message: Not quite. A line plot is for showing how a value changes over an ordered sequence (such as time). It is not designed for comparing distributions across groups.

opt_hist.message: Not quite. A histogram bins a single numeric variable to show its distribution shape. To compare distributions across multiple groups side by side, a box plot is the right choice.

correct.message: Exactly. A box plot gives a condensed display of each group's distribution — median, quartiles, whiskers, and outliers — all side by side.

incorrect.message: When you want to compare the full distribution (not just the average) across multiple groups, use a box plot. It shows the median, spread, and outliers for each group in a condensed side-by-side display.

opt_distort.message: Correct. With a baseline at 20, Kano's bar is 10 units tall and Lagos's is 5 units tall — Kano looks twice as long even though its average is only 5 minutes higher. The eye compares bar lengths from the baseline, so the baseline must be 0.

opt_fine.message: Not quite. Starting at a non-zero baseline distorts the comparison. Bar charts are easy to read because the eye compares lengths from a common baseline — if that baseline is not 0, the lengths no longer truthfully represent the values.

opt_missing.message: Not quite. A missing title is a labeling issue, not a baseline issue. The real problem is that starting bars at 20 instead of 0 makes Kano's bar look twice as long as Lagos's, distorting the comparison.

opt_wrong_type.message: Not quite. Bar charts can display any numeric value per category, including averages. The problem here is the non-zero baseline, which distorts the visual comparison of bar lengths.

correct.message: Exactly. A non-zero baseline makes bar lengths misleading — Kano's bar looks twice as long as Lagos's even though the difference is only 5 minutes. Keep the baseline at 0.

incorrect.message: Bar charts are easy to read because the eye compares lengths from a common baseline. If the baseline is not 0, the lengths distort the comparison. With a baseline at 20, Kano's bar (10 units) looks twice as long as Lagos's (5 units) even though the difference is only 5 minutes.

Sorts the delivery times and draws one bar per unique value
Computes the average delivery time and draws a single bar
Places one point per delivery time along the x-axis

opt_bin.message: Correct. `plt.hist()` uses `numpy.histogram` to bin the data in x, count the number of values in each bin, and draw the result as bars — one bar per bin.

opt_sort.message: Not quite. `plt.hist()` groups values into bins (ranges), not one bar per unique value. Drawing one bar per unique value would produce too many bars for continuous data.

opt_avg.message: Not quite. `plt.hist()` shows the distribution of all values, not a single summary. It bins the data and draws one bar per bin, showing how many values fall in each range.

opt_scatter.message: Not quite. Placing one point per value is what a scatter plot does. `plt.hist()` groups values into bins and draws one bar per bin, showing the count in each range.

correct.message: Right. `plt.hist()` uses `numpy.histogram` to bin the data and count values per bin, then draws one bar per bin — revealing the distribution shape.

incorrect.message: `plt.hist(x, bins=...)` uses `numpy.histogram` to bin the data in x, count the number of values in each bin, and draw the result as bars.

public.prompt: Which of the following is a valid way to call `plt.hist()` that sets explicit bin edges at 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 minutes?

options.text: `plt.hist(orders['delivery_time_minutes'], bins=[10, 20, 30, 40, 50])`
`plt.hist(orders['delivery_time_minutes'], bins=4)`
`plt.hist(orders['delivery_time_minutes'], bins='auto')`
`plt.hist(orders['delivery_time_minutes'])`

opt_seq.message: Correct. Passing a sequence sets explicit bin edges — here the four bins are [10, 20), [20, 30), [30, 40), and [40, 50], exactly as specified.

opt_int.message: Not quite. Passing an integer sets that many *equal-width* bins — the edges are computed automatically from the data range, not set explicitly. To set explicit edges, pass a sequence.

opt_auto.message: Not quite. Passing the string `'auto'` selects a binning strategy automatically — the edges are chosen by the algorithm, not set explicitly. To set explicit edges, pass a sequence.

opt_default.message: Not quite. Calling `plt.hist()` without a `bins` argument uses the default of 10 equal-width bins. To set explicit bin edges, pass a sequence such as `[10, 20, 30, 40, 50]`.

correct.message: Exactly. Passing a sequence to `bins` sets explicit bin edges — the four bins are [10, 20), [20, 30), [30, 40), and [40, 50].

incorrect.message: The `bins` parameter accepts three forms: an integer (equal-width bins), a sequence (explicit edges), or a string strategy such as `'auto'`. To set explicit edges at 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, pass a list.

hints: The question asks for *explicit* bin edges — which form of `bins` sets the edges directly?
An integer sets the *number* of bins; a sequence sets the *edges*.
